title: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse

keywords: the town mouse and the country mouse
full_text:
A humble Country Mouse who lived in an underground burrow beneath the roots of a wild hazel bush invited his aristocratic cousin, the Town Mouse, to visit him for dinner. The Country Mouse, proud of his hospitality, served the best provisions his pantry could afford: dried wheat stalks, wild berry seeds, and a hard crust of barley bread.

The Town Mouse turned up his whiskers with polite disdain, merely nibbling a seed or two. "My dear cousin," drawled the elegant visitor, "how can you endure such a dreary, monotonous existence among roots and chaff? Come with me to the grand city mansion where I reside! You shall dine upon rich cheeses, sweet pastries, and roasted meats fit for kings."

Enticed by visions of royal luxury, the Country Mouse accompanied his cousin to the city. That night, they crept into the mansion's vast dining hall, where a lavish banquet had just concluded. The Country Mouse gasped in wonder: tables groaned beneath silver platters of roast chicken, rich Brie cheese, jellies, and candied fruits.

"Eat your fill, cousin!" urged the Town Mouse grandly.

Just as the Country Mouse was sinking his teeth into a delectable cream tart, the heavy oak doors burst open with a crash. A ferocious mastiff and a sleek, sharp-clawed Persian cat bounded into the room, barking and hissing savagely!

The two mice fled in terror, scrambling frantically behind heavy draperies and squeezing through a crack in the skirting board, their tiny hearts pounding like drums. For two agonizing hours, they sat shivering in the dark, barely daring to breathe as claws scraped against the wainscot.

When quiet returned, the Country Mouse fetched his little walking stick. "Farewell, dear cousin," he whispered, heading for the garden door. "You may keep your silver platters, your rich tarts, and the terrifying terror that seasons every bite. Give me my simple barley crust and quiet safety in the meadow, where I may dine in uninterrupted peace!"
moral: A humble meal enjoyed in quiet peace is far superior to luxurious banquets seasoned with terror.
